value.text: A firefighter/paramedic died Saturday morning while on duty, one year after his brother, also with the St. Lucie County Fire District, passed away, the agency said. Austin Hodge joined the St. Lucie County Fire District on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies went from the hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. His brother, Jarius Hodge, died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered on May 30 to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday with a cookout and balloon release. Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 There are 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters, according to the agency's website. Information regarding memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge's service iwll be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized. "His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community," the agency said. "The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time." Several agencies offered their condolences, including Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, Port St. Lucie Police Department, Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0cPopWYk7mLx2z6QfJqkd99ZUoP9dWGSRx3Y7yjuN21oLAqBUmr6n8RYoUYP9RGaZl The St. Lucie agency thanked other agencieson Facebook. https://www.facebook.com/slcfd/posts/pfbid02FGoAgmLryFmnkCkLqRQfwhzpBpGAX3Bh285A6jFqKysGajonPUPDHeKjxdFm2KQvl "In the hours following this heartbreaking loss, our firefighters, Honor Guard, and public safety partners came together to honor our fallen brother and stand alongside one another during an incredibly difficult time. The brotherhood of the fire service extends far beyond the walls of a fire station. It is a bond built on trust, shared experiences, and an unwavering commitment to one another. "Today, that bond was especially evident through the incredible support of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves. Our hearts are with Austin’s family, loved ones, and everyone who had the privilege of serving alongside him. We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss." Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

A 5-year-old girl reported missing in Fort Pierce Saturday morning was found dead in a nearby body of water, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.Police announced the update at 4:13 p.m. Saturday, saying officers were on scene where the child had been located deceased.“Our deepest condolences are with [her] family and loved ones during this tragic time,” the department said.The girl was reported missing at approximately 11:39 a.m. 24.Police did not immediately provide additional information about the circumstances surrounding her death.

A severe thunderstorm Friday evening produced ping-pong- to golf-ball-sized hail in South Florida.We received several reports of the large hailstones in Riviera Beach, Lake Park, and North Palm Beach. Videos sent to our newsroom show hail being hurled into pools and ricocheting off driveways. WATCH: Severe storm drops ping-pong ball-sized hail across South FloridaThe storms also produced around 4 inches of rain in the West Palm Beach area.More heavy rainfall is in our forecast this weekend.FORECAST: Coastal flooding and gusty winds expected this weekend

A 20-year-old Bronx, New York, man was extradited to St. Lucie County after Canadian border authorities arrested him while he was trying to enter Canada , the Sheriff’s Office said. Gibrill Diallo faces charges of money laundering, a scheme to defraud of $50,000 or more and grand theft in connection with an investigation into a check stolen from a Port St. Lucie real estate company, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . The agency said the check was altered and deposited into a bank account opened using a stolen identity. Detectives traced the funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers before they were deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account, the Sheriff’s Office said. Authorities arrested Diallo on Oct. He was held at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. 21, according to the agency. See also: Boynton woman held on $20M bond, accused of selling high-THC products, money laundering Sheriff Richard Del Toro said detectives followed the money and pursued leads across jurisdictions.

NORAD and USNORTHCOM said ground-based air defense assets have been deployed in and around Mar-a-Lago.WPTV shot video of the new defense equipment at President Donald J. Trump International Airport.Watch video:“At the request of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and under NORAD and USNORTHCOM authorities, NORAD and USNORTHCOM deployed ground-based air defense assets in and around Mar-a-Lago, Florida. Due to security considerations, we cannot provide tactics, techniques and procedural specifics. For further detail, we refer you to the USSS,” the NORAD and USNORTHCOM spokesperson said.WPTV's Joel Lopez reported on Oct. 6 NORAD said more than 60 aircraft had been intercepted near Mar-a-Lago since Trump's return to office.

Palm Beach County election officials are urging voters to double-check their ballots after some early voters raised concerns about selections they say did not register the way they intended on ExpressVote ballot-marking devices.Boca Raton resident Ceil Friedenthal is one of them. She voted early Tuesday at the South County Civic Center and said she noticed the issue more than once.“I went to the machines and I pressed what I wanted and I used the tip of my finger, the pad of my finger, and a couple of times it defaulted to something I wasn't voting for,” Friedenthal said. “So if I voted for one party, it defaulted to the other, not every single time, but several.”Friedenthal said in her case she was attempting to select a Democratic candidate, but the Republican candidate listed above was selected instead.The experience immediately caught her attention.“I better get somebody over here to take a look at it because I don't know what to do,” she recalled.Friedenthal said she called a poll worker over three separate times because she caught three selections she believed were incorrect. Each time, she said a worker helped correct the issue.For Friedenthal, making sure those selections were right mattered more than simply getting through the voting process quickly.“Listen, in my opinion, as an ordinary U.S. citizen, the only thing we can do is vote,” she said. “There's really nothing else that we can do as an individual, so it's important that your vote be registered correctly.”Friedenthal also told WPTV she had spoken with two other women who said they experienced something similar while early voting.WPTV took Friedenthal's concerns directly to Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link.Link said her office had received only a couple of reports directly from voters.She stressed that when voters experience a problem, they should notify a poll worker immediately. That not only gives workers a chance to help the voter, but also allows election officials to identify the specific machine and test it.“We have the ability to immediately test that machine and see if we can recreate the problem,” Link said. “Obviously if there is an issue, we're going to replace that machine.”Link told WPTV election workers are also proactively checking the equipment.“We are throughout the day, if there's not a voter at a machine, we are proactively testing them again, making sure everything's properly calibrated,” Link said. “To this moment, we have not been able to recreate the problem.”In at least one instance where officials knew which machine a voter had used, Link said the office replaced it as a precaution.“When we did have a voter tell us we used, you know, X machine, then just to be safe, we went ahead and replaced that machine,” Link said. “We brought it back to our office, tried to recreate the problem using fingers, and we couldn't, so we don't think it was the machine, but again, in an abundance of caution, we did replace that one because we did know which one it was.”It was unclear which voting center that machine was located in.Elections office points to several possible factorsLink said there is no setting on an ExpressVote machine that defaults a voter to a particular candidate.Instead, Link said a voter's finger or fingernail can sometimes make contact with a different selection than intended.“If your fingernail is a little long, you might be thinking you're hitting one, but you're really hitting the selection above,” Link said. “Or if you happen to have large hands, maybe you're hitting two different types of selections.”Friedenthal disputes that explanation in her case.“No, I use the pad of my finger, not the nail itself, and I pressed twice with the pad, so the nail wasn't involved at all,” she said.While acknowledging that her fingernails are a little long, Friedenthal demonstrated to WPTV how she said she touched the screen.Link also pointed to the age and responsiveness of the ExpressVote equipment as another factor voters should keep in mind.“These machines are a little bit older. We're actually getting new ones,” Link said.She said the newer machines are expected to be used in March.“With the slower, a little bit slower technology, you may find that, like when you're used to hitting an iPhone, something, it shows up right away,” Link said. “And these may have just a slight delay from when you hit it before it acknowledges your selection.”Link said repeatedly touching the screen while waiting for it to respond could potentially result in a voter touching another selection.“So we just say give it a moment, let it make your selection, use the stylus,” Link said.The Supervisor of Elections Office is now emphasizing the use of the stylus available with the ExpressVote machines.“There's a stylus provided with every machine because with that stylus, it is, you know, it is smaller than your finger, and so you're not going to be hitting two areas at the same time,” Link said.Link said her office contacted poll workers after hearing the concerns and asked them to be more proactive about encouraging voters to use the stylus.She said styluses should be available at every machine, with extras available at check-in if one is missing.Friedenthal, however, told WPTV she did not remember seeing one when she voted.“I didn't see anything, and nobody suggested anything,” she said. “They didn't say to me when I checked in, ‘Please use the stylus.’”Voters also don't have to use an ExpressVote device. Link said every voter can choose between an ExpressVote machine and a traditional oval ballot.The ExpressVote itself does not tabulate the vote. Link described it as a ballot-marking device that produces a paper ballot.“It's called the Express Vote. That's the name of the machine, but yes, it's a ballot marking device,” Link said. “This does not tabulate the ballot. This actually just is marking your ballot.”Link stressed that voters using an ExpressVote have multiple opportunities to catch and correct a selection before their ballot is ultimately cast.If a voter notices an incorrect selection while using the device, Link said it can be corrected before printing the ballot. The machine also gives voters an opportunity to review their selections at the end of the process.“Then the voter has that chance to review all of those, and if they say, ‘No, I didn't want candidate A. I wanted candidate B,’ or what have you, then they have that opportunity to fix it right then,” Link said.After the paper ballot is printed, voters get another opportunity to review it.“Once they print out the paper ballot, then they can still review all of those selections again because it's printed for them,” Link said.If a voter still finds a mistake on the printed ballot, Link said they can bring it to a poll worker, spoil the ballot and receive another one.Her message to voters is simple: slow down, use the stylus if choosing the ExpressVote and check every selection.“Make sure that you're double-checking your selections, whether you're using the Express Vote or the oval ballots,” Link said. “So, just double check your selections no matter which method you're choosing to use.”That's also what Friedenthal wants other voters to take away from her experience.“Just be careful,” Friedenthal said. “Watch the screen and make sure you're getting what you want.”She said she hopes election officials continue looking into what happened.“I just want them to look into why this glitch is occurring and for people to be careful so their vote can be counted.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country.Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”RELATED STORY | Trump rules out attacking Iran before November's midterm electionsRubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba, addressing his post “to those who seek to create positive change” and urging them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”FOREIGN POLICY NEWS | Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelectionRubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership — was “deep into negotiations with Cuba,” saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal,” adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States.

Lucie police (PSLPD) said it has arrested a person in connection with an Oct. 9 hit-and-run crash that injured a 63-year-old man.The crash happened at around 12:56 a.m. near NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard."Our officers that work night we're used to seeing him out exercising in the evening and he was known to jog, walk in the street medians," Chief Leo Niemczyk said.The victim was identified through information on his Garmin watch and traced back to his home.PSLPD said the man was found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries, was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, and remains in critical condition."Watch report:Detectives reviewed surveillance video and additional evidence, identified Eric Saint Aude, 60, as a suspect, and arrested him, PSLPD said.He was arrested for leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

Lucie County firefighter died unexpectedly Saturday morning, prompting an outpouring of condolences from public safety agencies across the Treasure Coast.The St. Lucie County Fire District first announced the firefighter’s death Saturday, saying the department was “deeply saddened” by the loss.“Our thoughts are with the firefighter’s family, loved ones, and our fellow firefighters as we navigate this difficult loss,” the district said.The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office later said the firefighter “unexpectedly passed away this morning.”The Port St. Lucie Police Department also offered condolences to the firefighter’s family, friends and colleagues.“Behind every uniform is a person who has answered a calling greater than themselves,” the department said. “A life devoted to service, a commitment to protecting others, and a family who makes sacrifices alongside them.”Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk and the department said they stand with the St. Lucie County Fire District as it mourns.“When one of us grieves, we all grieve,” the department said.The firefighter’s identity and additional details surrounding his death have not been released.The St. Lucie County Fire District said further information will be released when appropriate.WPTV has reached out to the fire district for additional details.This is a developing story.

Lennar Homes' confirmation of its intent to buy the Boynton Beach Mall reflects a growing trend in which declining retail space is seen as an opportunity for housing developments. In a statement, Lennar Homes says, “Lennar expects to complete the purchase of the Boynton Beach Mall site early next year with plans to develop a vibrant mixed-use community that helps alleviate Palm Beach County’s severe housing shortage. Watch report from Matt Sczesny:Although planning is in the early stages and we look forward to stakeholder feedback, our vision is to take advantage of this unique opportunity with a mix of single-family attached housing opportunities, complemented by retail, commercial, open space and civic uses that will create a walkable, connected environment.” “In South Florida, we’re developed, there’s a need for housing and when we start looking for opportunities to do it, retail centers are an obvious choice to do that," says Eric Dumbaugh, at FAU's School of Urban and Regional Planning. In Vero Beach the Indian River Mall is being transformed into a mix use development.And in Palm Beach County, the unoccupied Nordstrom building at Wellington Mall is being viewed as a possible site for an apartment complex.As for the Boynton Beach Mall site, Dumbaugh says the location seems ideal.“I don’t know what affordable means in the South Florida market anymore but it's going to be a lot more affordable than what they expect to pay in a place like Delray or in Boca," Dumbaugh says.

The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died after the SUV he was driving collided with a semi-trailer at an intersection in Indian River County on Thursday. The crash happened as a 2026 Freightliner truck-tractor pulling a flatbed trailer attempted to turn left from a stop sign on westbound 49th Street, according to a crash report from the Florida Highway Patrol . The Freightliner entered the path of a northbound 2006 Dodge Durango traveling on 66th Avenue, and the front of the SUV struck the left side of the trailer. The Durango driver was taken to Health First’s Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead at 8:02 a.m. His next of kin had not been notified, according to the report. See also: West Palm Beach man faces up to life after conviction in child sex trafficking case The 59-year-old Jacksonville man driving the Freightliner did not report any injuries. The traffic homicide investigation is ongoing.

The child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver has ended after prosecutors declined to file formal charges. The State Attorney’s Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document. The filing listed the charge as child abuse intentional act, but did not explain why prosecutors decided not to proceed. Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The allegations were described in an arrest affidavit. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. The video, recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m., showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club, according to the affidavit. Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat. Alpy was seen walking through the aisle and directing the student to sit down. The student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned, the affidavit said. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student’s seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student again stood up and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down. When the child did not, she pulled the bus over, left the driver’s seat and approached the student. Investigators alleged she grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. See also: More than 4.3 million toothpaste tubes recalled, including children's brands The child’s middle finger was extended toward Alpy, according to the affidavit. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student’s hand, forced it into the child’s lap and asked, Do you want me to break this finger? The student later told investigators that Alpy grabbed and bent back the child’s middle finger and said she was going to break it off. The child said they were afraid during the encounter, according to the affidavit.

Lucie County Board of County Commissioners is partnering with the Treasure Coast Food Bank for a county-wide food drive Oct. Lucie County facilities will serve as donation drop-off sites for residents who want to donate shelf-stable food. The food bank’s most-needed items include canned vegetables and fruit, soups and stews, rice and grains, pasta and pasta sauce, tuna, peanut butter and jelly, cereal and snacks such as granola bars, crackers and nuts.St. Lucie County donation sites include the following locations: Dorothy J. Conrad Building, 1664 S.E. 34952 Roger Poitras County Admin Building, 2300 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce, Fla. 34982 (Use the north entrance on S. 25th Street or the west entrance on S. 23rd Street)Susan Broom Kilmer Branch Library, 101 Melody Lane, Fort Pierce, Fla. 34950Lakewood Park Branch Library, 7605 Santa Barbara Drive, Fort Pierce, Fla. Lewis Branch Library, 2950 S.W. 34953Morningside Branch Library, 2410 S.E. Morningside Blvd., Port St. 34952UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County, 8400 Picos Road, Suite 101, Fort Pierce, Fla. 34945The county said donations will support families in need in St. Lucie County through the Treasure Coast Food Bank.

A 60-year-old man was arrested in connection with a hit-and-run crash that critically injured a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. 9 on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Ft. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. He said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened. Investigators reviewed video, physical evidence and other leads since the crash two weeks ago. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant which sought cellphone location data from a specific area during a specific time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell phone towers in that area at the time of the crash. That helped detectives identify Aude as the alleged hit and run driver and the vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined the man’s vehicle, which had damage consistent with striking a pedestrian, including damage to the front bumper and hood, Niemczyk said. Investigators also found presumptive positive results for blood on the vehicle. Further testing is needed. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle’s inner fender-well fasteners at the scene, Niemczyk said. Detectives found that several matching fasteners were missing from the suspect’s vehicle. Investigators are still looking for a second vehicle that was traveling southbound near the crash. Niemczyk said distant video showed a vehicle traveling in each direction, but it was difficult to determine what happened. Police are trying to learn whether the second vehicle also struck the victim or if the driver of the second vehicle witnessed the accident. We’re very confident that the vehicle that we have and the person that we’ve arrested are responsible for the majority of what occurred, Niemczyk said. The Police Chief said the victim was in the middle of the road when he was struck, but investigators could not determine from the video whether he was walking or jogging. Police learned he often exercised at night when the weather was cooler and he was known to walk on the road and medians. "I've been doing this for 30 years. I'm not surprised by a whole lot anymore. I've seen pedestrians left for dead on the side of the road before. It doesn't make it any easier, but it doesn't surprise me at this point either. It's just difficult to understand how one human being could be so, you know, without compassion for another," Chief Niemczyk said. See also: 2 arrested in killing of transgender woman Jayla McGee in Belle Glade The victim had no identification or cellphone with him, Niemczyk said. Investigators used data from a Garmin exercise watch he was wearing to trace his route back to his house and were able to identify him. Niemczyk said the victim has significant head trauma and is unable to speak. He is expected to survive, but the chief said his quality of life may not be the same as it was before the crash. "An arrest cannot undo the harm or uncertainty imposed upon a victim, Niemczyk said, but it’s the first step in accountability. Police have not released a description of the southbound vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. Aude is being held on $45,000 bond.

Lucie have arrested a suspect in connection with a hit-and-run crash two weeks ago on NW California Boulevard that left a 63-year-old man critically injured and in the ICU. Authorities said the victim was exercising when a man, allegedly on his way to work to deliver newspapers, struck him with his car and fled the scene heading north. Surveillance footage appears to show the suspect driving away after the crash. "It’s a sad thing to see; there’s not many people that we see at this time," said a man who works nearby. Police identified the suspect as 60-year-old Eric Saint Aude. Investigators said nearby surveillance footage helped them identify the type of car involved, but the key breakthrough came from the suspect’s phone. Officers obtained a warrant to track phone pings in the area during the time of the crash, which led them to Aude. When officers located the suspect’s vehicle, they found damage on the front and blood evidence, according to police. Investigators questioned Aude about the crash. "He didn't display much emotion," said Chief Leo Niemczyk. "The victim has serious head trauma, which occurred at the point of impact." Police are still searching for a second vehicle they believe was heading south at the time of the crash. It’s rare that anything like that would happen, and the fact that it did, we need to raise awareness that we have to be more careful here," a nearby worker said. The victim remains in critical condition in the ICU, according to the chief. Police are asking anyone with information about the crash to contact them. A 20-year-old Bronx, New York, man was extradited to St. Lucie County after Canadian border authorities arrested him while he was trying to enter Canada , the Sheriff’s Office said. Gibrill Diallo faces charges of money laundering, a scheme to defraud of $50,000 or more and grand theft in connection with an investigation into a check stolen from a Port St. Lucie real estate company, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . The agency said the check was altered and deposited into a bank account opened using a stolen identity. Detectives traced the funds through multiple bank accounts and Zelle transfers before they were deposited into Diallo’s personal bank account, the Sheriff’s Office said. Authorities arrested Diallo on Oct. He was held at the Niagara County Jail in New York before being extradited to St. 21, according to the agency. Questions about who is leading Riviera Beach and the future of City Manager William E. Wilkins took center stage during a contentious city council discussion Wednesday, as some elected leaders said they were unaware of the extent of his absence following an August car crash.Wilkins has been working remotely since the crash, according to city officials. While assistant city manager staff have handled many day-to-day operations inside city hall, some council members said they only recently learned key details about Wilkins' condition and work arrangements.The debate comes as Riviera Beach continues to navigate leadership challenges following the April 2026 firing of former City Manager Jonathan Evans, with residents and officials alike calling for stability at City Hall.WATCH: Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, statusCouncil members question communication and leadershipDuring Wednesday's meeting at Marina Village, some council members expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of communication regarding Wilkins' status.Councilwoman Shirley D. Lanier said she had not spoken with Wilkins since August and was unaware he had been injured in a crash."I didn't know he was in a car wreck. I didn't know he was on TV and I haven't heard from him since then," Lanier said.Lanier and Councilwoman Kashamba Miller-Anderson questioned whether the city's leadership structure is sustainable if the city manager remains out of the office for an extended period."I understand he has health issues. But someone has to run the business of the city," Lanier said during the discussion.Miller-Anderson argued that city leaders need clarity on Wilkins' plans moving forward. Miller-Anderson also questioned whether Wilkins' remote work arrangement aligns with the terms of his employment agreement."Either take leave, resign, or come back. And I think that's only right and that's only fair to ask," Miller-Anderson said.Other officials say city operations continueNot everyone on the dais agreed with the criticism.Dr. Glen Spiritis, chair pro tem, said he has maintained communication with Wilkins and believes the city manager continues to oversee city operations while working remotely."I have had communications with him, and he is clearly in charge right now," Spiritis said, while also praising the assistant city manager's handling of daily operations.Supporters argued that city business remains on track despite Wilkins' recovery and remote work arrangement.Residents call for stabilitySeveral residents who spoke during or around the meeting said they were largely unaware of the circumstances surrounding Wilkins' absence.Resident Doretta Paulk said she did not know what had happened to the city manager."This is a very sad situation because I didn't even know what happened to Mr. Wilkins," Paulk said.Other residents urged city leaders to focus on moving Riviera Beach forward rather than engaging in disputes."We're here for the business of the city," resident Margaret Shepherd said. "Let's find out how we can move the city forward."What happens next?City officials are set to review potential next steps regarding Wilkins' status. It remains unclear whether any formal action will be considered by the city council.WPTV reached out to Wilkins for comment but had not received a response as of Wednesday evening.The discussion is likely to remain a topic of public interest as city leaders work to provide clarity on Riviera Beach's management structure and long-term leadership plans.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County State Attorney Alexcia Cox announced Friday that a grand jury indicted Hugh Earp Milner Jr. on charges of first-degree murder with a firearm, attempted second-degree murder with a firearm, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and shooting into an occupied vehicle.The charges stem from the Sept. 27 shooting death of 31-year-old Akeem Moore, a local minister and musician.According to investigators, officers responded to reports of a shooting shortly before 3 a.m. 27 in the area of 45th Street and Australian Avenue. Moore was found suffering from gunshot wounds inside a vehicle and was pronounced dead at a hospital.Detectives later identified Hugh Earp Milner Jr. as the suspected gunman and obtained an arrest warrant. Investigators said Moore had been sitting in the driver's seat of a vehicle with another person when gunfire erupted. The passenger survived the shooting.Moore, known throughout the community for his ministry and music, was remembered by friends and family as a mentor who worked to inspire young people and strengthen his community. A vigil held in the days following his death drew dozens of mourners.According to the State Attorney's Office, the indictment follows an investigation by the West Palm Beach Police Department.In a statement announcing the charges, Cox described the killing as a senseless act of violence."Akeem Moore was a young man who served the community through his ministry and his music," Cox said. "This senseless act of violence leaves lasting pain for those who knew and loved him. My office remains committed to holding violent offenders accountable and seeking justice on behalf of victims. This indictment serves as a critical first step."Milner was previously arrested in connection with the shooting and appeared in Palm Beach County court earlier this month.The case will now be prosecuted by the Homicide Unit of the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office.

— A celebrity golf tournament in Palm Beach County brought athletes, community leaders, and supporters together for a day on the course, but the larger goal stretched far beyond golf.Par for the Culture, presented by the Higher Learning Foundation, raised support for The Lord’s Place and its efforts to expand housing and early-intervention services for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County.The need is significant.The Lord’s Place says the county has more than 500 shelter beds dedicated to people experiencing homelessness, while roughly 1,500 people currently need housing.Those existing beds are generally prioritized for people with the greatest needs, including those who have experienced homelessness for longer periods of time or face significant health and safety concerns.That can leave people who are newly unhoused waiting for help -a gap The Lord’s Place hopes to address with a new shelter model focused on early intervention.The goal is to provide intensive, short-term support before a temporary housing crisis becomes long-term homelessness.“We would really love to shorten their experience in homelessness and get them bridged back and transitioned back into the community as quickly as possible,” said Christine Frederick, CEO of The Lord’s Place.Outreach workers say intervening early can help people maintain jobs, stay in school, address health needs and preserve the support systems that can help them regain stability.Cristina Lucier with The Lord’s Place said the longer someone remains on the streets, the greater the risk of losing those connections.“The longer people spend on the streets, they may lose some of those critical social connections that will help them get back on their feet and retain stability long term,” Lucier said.For Devin Perry, that instability was once part of everyday life.“The hardest part is knowing where you’re gonna sleep at, where you’re gonna wake up at, if your stuff is gonna be there when you come back,” Perry said.Perry later entered The Lord’s Place culinary training program, secured housing and began moving toward employment.Having a place of his own has changed what he is able to think about each day.“When the weather is changing, I don’t have to worry about getting sheets or blankets or when it’s too hot, I don’t have to worry about getting fans,” Perry said. “I have some place to call my own.”That type of stability is exactly what organizers behind Par for the Culture hope to help create for more people.Founder Darren Wingate said he created the event as a way to combine his love of golf with community impact.“I just thought, like, hey, why not through the game of golf to spread the message with something that we love as a sport, and also as a community to give back and show progress as well,” Wingate said.The event brought athletes and community leaders to Palm Beach National Golf Club in Greenacres, with proceeds benefiting The Lord’s Place and its housing initiatives.Wingate said the larger mission is to remind participants that their impact can extend far beyond sports.“It’s more than sports. It’s home, shelter, community, all those things,” he said.For The Lord’s Place, the hope is that support generated on the golf course can ultimately help more people find a path back to permanent housing and a place they can call home.For more information on the services The Lord's Place provides you can click here to learn more.

Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school.Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school.On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students."It scares me," parent Kendall George said. "These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus."Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone."We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention," Ribaudo said. "Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic."At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call."Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt," Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "You will absolutely get a school zone."School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area."The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased," Rynca said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.""It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. In a statement they said:In the meantime, these parents are asking drivers to be cautious."Slow down if you see a school — even if there's not a school zone sign, slow down," Ribaudo said.With a school zone on the horizon, these parents said the next step is getting better street lighting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WPTV is staying on top of the future of data centers in Palm Beach County as commissioners rethink who should help develop new regulations for an industry that has already generated significant concern among residents.County commissioners on Wednesday backed away from immediately moving forward with one consultant selected by staff, instead deciding they want to consider other options before making a final selection.At the same time, commissioners agreed to bring back plans for a formal community task force, giving the public a greater role as the county considers what its future data center regulations should look like.The discussion comes less than a month after commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on Sept. 24.County staff told commissioners the clock is now running to establish regulations before that moratorium expires.The county staff had proposed hiring VHB (Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.), an engineering and planning firm, to work alongside staff on a framework designed to protect communities, establish clearer expectations and create standards the county could administer and enforce.It would cost $224,900 for VHB's services.But the proposal quickly drew questions from residents.“I have concerns today about the consultant who was chosen,” said Rachel Smith, an Acreage resident.Resident Ben Brown questioned how the firm had been selected and whether enough alternatives were considered.“I have many questions. When did you reach out to this consultant? Are you interviewing other ones?” Brown said. “They obviously work with data centers. You are putting the fox in the henhouse.”County staff said they issued a request for information and received six proposals that were incomplete. Staff initially told commissioners the proposals ranged from $200,000 for a portion of the needed support to $2 million.Later in the discussion, staff described the range as about $125,000 for an architect who would only be part of the process, requiring additional experts, to about $2.1 million.Those concerns put particular scrutiny on VHB and its existing work involving data centers.“Do you have clients that are a part of data centers?” Mayor Sara Baxter asked the consultant representative directly.“We work for clients that have data centers in Massachusetts and Virginia,” answered Curt Ostrodka a VHB representative responded. “We don't have any clients in Florida building data centers.”The firm's representative also told commissioners VHB had worked as a consultant for private clients providing civil engineering, utility studies and other technical services supporting data centers.When Commissioner Gregg Weiss asked whether the company had ever developed regulations specifically for data centers, the answer was direct.“Not for data centers," said Ostrodka.VHB maintained it could serve as an objective third party while researching how other communities are handling data centers and studying potential impacts including noise, energy and water.“We don't know the answers right now,” Ostrodka said. “We would do that collaboratively with staff, members of the public.”The company outlined a nine-month process that would also examine applicable state and federal laws and determine thresholds and regulatory mechanisms for potential impacts.Commissioner Maria Sachs was among those who wanted more information before committing to the firm.“This is one company standing here I know nothing about,” Sachs said.But county staff stressed that the push to hire a consultant isn't simply about getting another opinion. Staff told commissioners they need additional capacity and technical expertise to develop the rules.“We are asking for this assistance because we are limited in our capacity to do the work,” staff told commissioners. “We need the technical expertise to help support the staff get this done.”Commissioner Joel Flores asked what it might cost for the county to instead bring in its own people to handle the workload.Staff estimated a dedicated team could require two employees, with an average annual salary of about $125,000 each, or roughly $250,000.Flores said the need for specialized knowledge was part of the reason he supported hiring outside help.“I'm not an expert on data centers and this technology is evolving so quick,” Flores said.Flores said commissioners will ultimately decide what the county's rules look like, but expert information could help them determine what safeguards are necessary.“Having someone on our side who is going to say these are the things you want to watch out for, these are the guardrails you want to put in place, I would feel more comfortable,” Flores said.For some residents, the concern was less about whether the county hires a consultant and more about making sure it hires the right one.“For me, at least, it’s less of a money issue and more of, I want quality information, not just necessarily what people want to hear,” Wellington resident Elizabeth Pandich said. “I want to make sure we pick a consultant that is maybe in an environmental and scientific aspect of it, not someone that’s just good at moving data around.”The timeline also weighed heavily on the discussion.Staff told commissioners the moratorium lasts a year. If it expires before the county has new regulations in place, data center applications would be handled under the regulations in place at that time. County attorneys said extending the moratorium could be possible under certain circumstances, but any extension would be limited.Weiss put the urgency bluntly.“Time is of the essence. The clock is ticking,” Weiss said.What initially appeared to be a decision to move forward with VHB changed dramatically near the end of the discussion.Commissioners first voted to proceed with the consultant, with Baxter and Sachs opposed. But moments later, Commissioner Bobby Powell moved to reconsider the decision.Powell said he wanted commissioners to have choices before committing to a single company.“My motion is not to consider two consultants,” Powell said. “It would be for us to have an option to not only consider this consultant but more options. One consultant, maybe there is another person or another consultant company.”The motion to reconsider passed 3-2.Commissioners then voted 4-1 to give the county the opportunity to look at other available consultants rather than immediately settling on VHB.That doesn't necessarily mean VHB is out of consideration.“I'm sure this gentleman may win out in the end,” Sachs said. “But then at least we would know. Let's find out.”While commissioners debated which experts should advise them, there was considerably more agreement about giving residents a direct role in the process.Several speakers called for commissioners to revive the idea of a community task force, arguing that the two public outreach meetings outlined by staff would not provide enough community involvement.Baxter supported establishing a formal task force and suggested that because the regulations would apply countywide, each commissioner could appoint someone to represent their district.“This new ordinance, it would be countywide,” Commissioner Marci Woodward said earlier in the discussion. “This isn't about a specific parcel.”Baxter said the task force proposal could come back before commissioners at their Nov. 18 meeting.Smith welcomed the idea of combining expert input with residents who could be affected by whatever rules the county ultimately adopts.“I do appreciate that they are looking at expert opinions, although I do think that we have enough experts in this area who are actually affected that could be very beneficial,” Smith said.Pandich said she and others who became involved after Project Tango have already formed the National Data Impact Coalition and hope to participate.“I’m excited about the task force. A couple of friends of mine, after Project Tango, started a national data impact coalition, and we are doing that basically internally. So we are going to put our name in the hat and hopefully get a seat at the table,” Pandich said.For Smith, commissioners' decision to take another look at the consultant while moving toward giving residents a more formal role represented progress.“Yeah, I’d say it’s a victory for the residents,” Smith said. “Thank you to Sachs and Baxter for doing what they did, and Powell, who came in last minute and saved the day.”WPTV reached out to VHB to address concerns raised during the meeting about potential conflicts of interest but has not received a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. On any given Tuesday or Thursday night in the fall, you can expect to see nearly 300 young athletes playing softball at Lake Charleston Park in western Palm Beach County. Two local nonprofits are giving more young athletes the chance to play the sport, with a goal of expanding softball in a way that is affordable and accessible to all.One of those programs is the VSA Lady Lions, a travel softball program whose under-14s team runs a practice packed full of every element softball has to offer — from the tee to home plate."Our normal practice starts with stretching, throwing," Coach Ed Kunzweiler said. "They do a lot of defensive drills. Then we usually do some hitting off coaches, and then we usually try to finish with some live hitting," Kunzweiler said.Coach Kunzweiler said when he started at the club, they had just two travel teams."Now we're at 8 or 9. So it's grown pretty substantially," Kunzweiler said.He said the VSA Lady Lions are the largest women's travel softball program in South Florida — and interest is still growing."I'm really proud about what we built here. It's something that has grown every season," Kunzweiler said.One of the program's star players is Ari Merklein, who plays shortstop, third base and some outfield. She admits her favorite spot on the field is shortstop."I got involved in softball because I just didn't know what sport to pick when I was little and I just couldn't get used to 1 sport. But then I joined softball and I made a lot of friends and I got really good at it and just continued doing it," Merklein said.She never looked back. Merklein said that whether it's at practice or traveling to tournaments on the weekend, her team is having fun."It's really fun. We're all like good friends with each other, so we all hang out outside of softball and inside of softball, and we're good at communicating with each other. So it's just like a lot of good teamwork," Merklein said.Just a field away are the softball newbies who are part of West Boynton Girls Fastpitch, a recreational softball program that is beginner-friendly and has around 200 participants this year."We have kids out here right now that are four or five years old, just learning to pick up a softball for the very first time,” Coach Kunzweiler said. "It's a special program."A place to start — and a place to grow. For many players, that pathway begins with recreational softball.West Boynton Girls Fastpitch provides girls across multiple age groups and experience levels an opportunity to learn the fundamentals of the game, compete locally and become part of a softball community."What's exciting to me is coming by here and seeing all four fields being used. Whether it's rec or travel, it doesn't really matter, but to me, that's what youth sports is supposed to be like, especially community local sports, and it's exciting. We're giving these kids opportunities,” Coach Kunzweiler said.From players learning the fundamentals to athletes like Merklein who want to play at the college level, softball in Lake Charleston Park is a team effort.The West Boynton Girls Fastpitch recreational program and the VSA Lady Lions travel teams are nonprofits and are offered free or at low cost — so that every young girl who picks up a bat can swing for the fences. To learn more about the VSA Lady Lions visit their website.

After noticing worsening water quality while rowing, South Fork High School senior Bianca Bernhard founded the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative (MORI) a student-led nonprofit that recycles oyster shells to support restoration projects in local waterways.“The water quality got really bad,” Bernhard told WPTV’s T.A. “That’s due to discharges from Lake Okeechobee, so I decided to do something with the extra free time.”The initiative, known as MORI, collects oyster shells from local restaurants. Volunteers at South Fork High School then help dry and cure the shells so they can be used in restoration projects.WATCH: Stuart student leads oyster restoration mission“I recycle a lot of shells from local restaurants,” Bernhard said. “These local shells will help create new reef structures like what I’m holding right here, and those reef structures will grow new oysters which will filter the water.”South Fork High School students and teachers have joined Bernhard’s conservation effort through the school’s marine science, construction and agriculture programs.During the WPTV segment, Jennifer Inostroza, a teacher at South Fork High School, explained that the school helps cure and dry the oyster shells so they are ready for future projects.Information provided by the Martin County School District says MORI has recruited more than 60 students and teachers and amassed approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shell.The district says participating students can earn honor credits through South Fork High School’s Marine Sciences program.The recycled shells do not immediately return to the water. They must first be transported, dried and cured before they can be incorporated into approved restoration structures.According to Bernhard, those structures provide places where new oysters can grow. She said the oysters then help filter and clean the surrounding water.MORI is also collaborating with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit that installs vertical oyster gardens. According to Bernhard’s Go Blue Awards narrative, shells cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the creation of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.Bernhard is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s 2026 Go Blue Awards.“Bianca is one of our finalists for the Go Blue Hatchling Awards,” said Audrey Padgett, VP of Marketing, at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, told WPTV. “We’ve had nominees from all over the world. So it’s really amazing to see someone selected by this independent panel of judges here in our backyard for the work that she’s doing to improve ocean conservation and ecosystems right here.”The annual awards recognize young people, individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations making contributions to ocean conservation.The 2026 Go Blue Awards ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. 30, at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach.Bernhard’s work comes as MORI prepares for its next phase. According to her Go Blue Awards narrative, she aims to expand the initiative to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.She also plans to pursue oyster restoration research with the Florida Oceanographic Society and work with students to develop additional structures for restoration projects.For Bernhard, the project began with something she saw while rowing. It has since grown into a broader effort that gives students a hands-on role in responding to the environmental challenges facing their community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award to recognize her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.
