cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case: Police Still Weighing Charges
cards.teaser: More than 100 cats rescued from a Port St. Lucie hoarding situation are recovering at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, where staff describe widespread flea infestations, ear mites and respiratory illness. Police say they are still deciding whether to file criminal charges against the owner.
cards.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, and police say they are still determining whether to file criminal charges against the owner. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, described the condition of the animals when they arrived. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care while others remain at the shelter. Wees said shelter staff cannot always tell which kittens belong to which mother because the cats were all living together in the same house. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was on site within days of being contacted. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. She said the cats are showing significant improvement under the added care. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said.

Port St. Lucie police continue to monitor the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed against the owner. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as treatment continues.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Weighs Chief Jeff Lee's Future After No-Confidence Vote
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board was scheduled to discuss Fire Chief Jeff Lee's future at its regular 3 p.m. meeting Wednesday, two weeks after the district's firefighters union released a no-confidence vote against top leadership. The board's agenda, listed under Chair Shannon Martin, includes an item titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not specify whose retirement would be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public.

The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released the vote results earlier in October. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence, a 74.23% no-confidence share. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the result would be formally presented to the board. Gonzalez and Sabol both cleared that threshold. The union said in its release that it calls on the board to carefully consider the results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve the county and the public they have sworn to protect.

Since the vote, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role, which the district said both Gonzalez and Lee agreed to and had discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days' notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire in December. Wednesday's agenda also includes selection of a law firm and a new district attorney.

The no-confidence vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district fired three veteran firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others after videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing, though the firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief, with board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler saying at an Oct. 6 meeting that the district cannot investigate itself. Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district's insurance representatives. Lee has said the board must fix the lack of a complaints policy because it is not a problem he can solve himself. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. A motion in August to suspend Lee and Sabol failed on a 2 to 4 vote. The district said after the no-confidence vote that it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action, pointing to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee's tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. military and became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. In 2017, after a similar union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

hero.headline: Indian River Sheriff Witnesses Execution of Deputy's 1986 Killer
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves on Tuesday night at Florida State Prison. Reaves was convicted of killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. He was quickly arrested after the crime and sentenced to death, and that sentence held through a retrial and multiple appeals.

Flowers said he deliberately positioned himself in the front row of the viewing area so Reaves would be able to see him. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I'm glad that he saw that," Flowers said. The execution lasted about 12 minutes. Reaves did not give a final statement, and his last meal was crackers and juice.

"The real kicker on top of it was that he didn't say anything; he didn't make a last statement; he didn't say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. It was the first execution Flowers had ever witnessed. He described the moment as the closing of a long chapter for his agency and for Raczkowski's family, but said it did not amount to true justice.

"It's closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," he added. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office plans to unveil a monument next month honoring its two fallen deputies.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case: Shelter Details Scale of Medical Care
hero.body:
More than 100 cats rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now undergoing extensive medical treatment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, which says the animals arrived suffering from upper respiratory infections, ear mites, fleas and open sores. Port St. Lucie Animal Control removed the cats over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. Police previously confirmed that 124 cats were taken from the home, some found dead, and that two residents were cited for hoarding and failing to provide medical care. Police are still determining whether criminal charges will be filed.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said the cats arrived in poor physical condition. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one of them was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care while other kittens remain at the shelter.

The scale of the intake has created confusion over which kittens belong to which mother. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. To manage the surge, the shelter is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters.

Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was deployed to the shelter within days of being contacted. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the cats are showing significant improvement under the added care. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as treatment continues.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue Honors Madison Isler With First Heroic Heart Award
hero.teaser: Nearly two months after a Martin County woman used CPR to help save a drowning 3-year-old, Martin County Fire Rescue honored her rescue efforts and reunited her with the child she saved.
hero.body:
Madison Isler, a 20-year-old Martin County woman, was honored with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award nearly two months after she used CPR to help save 3-year-old Luna, who was found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. The award ceremony, held at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters, reunited Isler with Luna for the first time since the Aug. 23 rescue.

The rescue happened as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex and noticed something unusual in the water. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." Isler said she jumped in and pulled Luna out, and the girl was blue and motionless. She called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, drawing on training she learned years earlier from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool." A family friend who works as a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said the two continued their efforts until Luna responded. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.

At the recognition ceremony, Cianciulli presented Isler with the department's inaugural Heroic Heart Award. "Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said. According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive the award.

Isler said the recognition mattered less to her than seeing Luna alive and thriving. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said. Isler calls Luna her "unicorn baby." Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she remains grateful that Isler was nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family."

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves Tuesday evening, 40 years after he shot and killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison at 6:12 p.m. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals.

According to court records, Raczkoski responded to the store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. The deputy's son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, saying he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant in September.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers pushed the governor to sign the warrant and witnessed the execution.

Reaves' attorneys fought the execution to the end, arguing in court filings that he was a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. DeSantis denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Florida Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, friend and spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Crews Battle Two Structure Fires in Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District crews battled two separate structure fires Monday, one on 17th Street in Fort Pierce and another on Aragon Lane in Port St. Lucie, with firefighters displacing residents at both properties while also rescuing a cat from the Aragon Lane home during the response. The two fires were part of a busy day for the district, which handled 215 calls for service Monday, and the American Red Cross is now assisting the families affected by both incidents.

Firefighters moved quickly at both scenes, bringing the flames under control and limiting how far they spread, according to the fire district. That rapid response helped reduce the amount of damage at each property. The district has not released further details about what sparked either fire or how extensive the damage turned out to be at the two homes.

The rescue at the Aragon Lane property stood out among the day's calls, as crews pulled a cat from the burning structure during their work to contain the fire. Beyond the rescue, the district has not provided additional specifics on the condition of the residents or the pet, nor has it detailed how many people were forced out of their homes as a result of the two fires.

With residents from both the Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie properties displaced, the American Red Cross stepped in to provide support as families navigate finding temporary housing and replacing lost belongings. The fire district credited its crews with containing both incidents swiftly despite the volume of calls they were managing across the county that day. Handling 215 calls in a single day reflects the kind of workload the district regularly faces, and Monday's structure fires were just two of the many emergencies firefighters responded to as part of that total.

The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to serve as the primary emergency response agency for fire and rescue calls throughout the county, routinely managing a high volume of incidents ranging from structure fires to medical emergencies and other calls for service. Monday's events underscore the kind of rapid-response work crews carry out on a daily basis, often juggling multiple serious incidents at once while still working to protect both residents and their pets. The district has not indicated whether any firefighters were injured during either response or whether investigators plan to release more information on the causes of the fires in the coming days.

hero.headline: Southeast County Line Road Bridge Closes for Year-Long $7M Rebuild in Martin County
hero.body:
A bridge on Southeast County Line Road in southern Martin County is now closed for a year-long reconstruction project expected to cost $7 million, with state and federal grants covering $6 million of that total. A road block is now in place notifying drivers to turn around, and officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route while the detour is in effect.

George May, who lives just off Southeast County Line Road, said the closure will take some adjustment for residents and commuters alike. "It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club," May said. May already drives over an hour to work each day and expects the detour to add about 20 minutes to his commute.

Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said the project involves extensive coordination because of utility work at the site. "There are a lot of utilities ther," Aveni said. "There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time." The new bridge will stand two feet higher than the current structure and will use a more resilient type of rebar designed to improve safety. Aveni said crews also plan to eliminate a sharp curve before the bridge and soften the approach, a change he said will make the area safer for pedestrians as well as drivers.

Despite the inconvenience, residents say they support the investment after watching the old bridge deteriorate. May said he had noticed large cracks underneath the structure before the closure began. Daniel Von, another area resident, said the temporary disruption is worth the upgrade. "It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that, to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area," Von said. May said his main hope now is that the county sticks to its timeline. "I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule," he said.

Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, saying he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state.

A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant in September and denied clemency the same day. Reaves' attorneys fought the execution to the end, arguing in court filings that he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the death warrant, planned to witness the execution in uniform. The brother told Flowers that "Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed." The Florida Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, a friend and his spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. Tuesday after Florida carried out his execution by lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke, closing out a four-decade case over the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. The execution was Florida's 18th of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeal without comment Tuesday afternoon.

According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged he had placed that call from a payphone outside the store. While the two men spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts and they struggled over it. Reaves regained control of the weapon, and investigators said the deputy tried to run away before Reaves shot him four times. Raczkowski later died from his wounds.

Reaves was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court later reversed that conviction over a conflict of interest involving the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and his subsequent appeals failed. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his final appeals last week.

Reaves' attorneys had challenged Florida's three-drug lethal injection protocol, which uses a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, a method the state's courts have previously upheld against similar challenges. Defense attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled due to post-traumatic stress disorder from his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday asking him to halt the execution.

Florida Department of Corrections spokesman Jordan Kirkland said Reaves woke at 5 a.m. Tuesday and remained compliant throughout the day. His last meal was crackers and juice, and he met with four visitors, including his sister, his brother, his nephew and a friend, along with a spiritual adviser. Reaves was the eighth Florida death row inmate over age 70 executed this year. Florida set a state record with 19 executions last year, and another execution, that of Jesse Guardado, 64, convicted of robbing and killing a woman in 2004, is scheduled for November and would tie that record if carried out as planned.

hero.headline: 124 Cats, Some Dead, Removed From Port St. Lucie Home in Hoarding Case
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police recovered 124 cats, living and deceased, from a home in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street as part of a criminal hoarding investigation. Two of the three residents of the home have been cited for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, according to police.

Animal Control personnel responded to the home on October 13 after receiving concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions. Inside, they documented accumulated feces and found deceased kittens. Police said the investigation remains active and have not released details about potential future arrests.

All 124 cats have been surrendered and are now receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas, while others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care. Some of the animals were transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Police said many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed.

The case has required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

cards.headline: Humane Society of St. Lucie County Seeks Help After Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case
cards.teaser: More than 120 cats and kittens were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County says the rescue has overwhelmed its staff and resources.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found inside a home in the 2500 block of Warwick Street, where investigators discovered unsanitary conditions including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens. Two of the three people living in the home were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County took in 106 of the cats and kittens, and the organization says the influx has doubled its cat population and strained its ability to care for the animals.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said the cats likely had to compete for food, leaving some underweight, and some nursing kittens may have been feeding from the wrong mother. "If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now," Wees said. She said almost all of the cats arrived with fleas and ear mites, and some had open sores requiring immediate medical treatment.

Staff and volunteers are now working to stabilize the animals. "They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes," Wees said. Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are improving quickly, pointing to their liveliness and eagerness to approach workers and take food. Still, Wees said some of the animals remain in a dangerous condition and are being treated in the shelter's sick room. "They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation," Wees said. "Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time."

Wees said the case has overwhelmed both staff and resources at the shelter. "It overwhelms the staff," Wees said. "It overwhelms our resources." The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking the community for donations, volunteers and foster homes to help with the recovery effort. "These little babies can't do it for themselves," Wees said. "So, we and the community need to do it for them." Once the cats and kittens receive the medical care they need, they will be made available for adoption.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Brings Governor Bus Tour to Fort Pierce College Campus
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds stopped at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center in Fort Pierce, joined by Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall to rally voters ahead of election day.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate and Congressman Byron Donalds stopped in Fort Pierce on Tuesday as part of a statewide bus tour, holding a campaign event at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center. Donalds was joined by his running mate for lieutenant governor, Bryan Avila, along with Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall, as the group worked to drive voter turnout in the final stretch before election day.

"I think for us we're just focused on making sure we drive turnout to the polls," Donalds said.

The Fort Pierce stop came in the middle of Tuesday's leg of the bus tour, which began in Melbourne and later continued to Miami. Donalds and Avila held a meet and greet in front of the campaign bus outside the Eastman Workforce Center, taking photos and talking with supporters who gathered at the stop.

"We show up, we stand outside, we take pictures with you, sign the bus, we have conversations with the voters. We've been consistently doing that for months now on the campaign trail. We're going to continue to do it every single day. I think the symbolism of the bus tour, it just helps people know that you're out here working hard for their vote and you want their support," Donalds said.

Donalds also laid out the economic message he has carried throughout the campaign, telling the Fort Pierce crowd that affordability for families and seniors remains central to his pitch to voters.

"We want our kids to achieve the Florida dream for themselves. We want to make sure it's affordable for our seniors and our working families in our state. That's what we've been laser focused on this entire time. We haven't gotten off of that," Donalds said.
